According to the Q2 Barclays Business Prosperity Index1, six in 10 businesses surveyed (60 per cent) have either increased investment to adapt to extreme heat (37 per cent) or are considering doing so (23 per cent).
The most common investment from firms is upgrading cooling equipment including air conditioning and ventilation (28 per cent). Close to a quarter (23 per cent) are adopting energy efficiency measures to manage the higher energy use.
Barclays anonymised client data also points to rising demand for cooling infrastructure, with air conditioning supplier businesses seeing cash inflows into Barclays accounts increase by 4.3 per cent year-on-year in Q2 2026.
Meanwhile, businesses are also adapting how their teams work during hotter periods, with 28 per cent introducing employee wellbeing measures such as additional breaks, 23 per cent offering flexible or remote working, and 21 per cent adjusting working hours.
The findings come as over a quarter (27 per cent) of small and micro businesses report that hot weather has had a negative impact on productivity. However larger businesses have proved more resilient, with almost half (47 per cent) citing a positive impact on productivity from the warmer weather.
Hot Weather Changes Consumer Demand And Trading Conditions
The effect of hotter weather is not limited to business operations. Consumer data suggests it is also changing demand and trading conditions for customer-facing businesses, particularly in retail.
According to the Barclays Consumer Spend report2, which combines hundreds of millions of customer transactions with consumer research, consumer card spending grew by 2.0 per cent year-on-year in July, following a 1.9 per cent uplift in June, although this remained below the latest CPIH inflation rate of 2.8 per cent.
Within retail, July’s heat was reflected in higher spending at garden centres and on clothing, which both rose 2.4 per cent, while electronic stores were up 1.5 per cent. The shift in clothing spend comes as one in five consumers (20 per cent) said they bought light and cool summer clothes in response to the heatwave.
When asked, UK adults chose 24.6°C as their ideal summer temperature, 13.1°C lower than 2026’s record high. This drops further when considering different activities, with consumers claiming 25.1°C is their maximum temperature for shopping.
Barclays Business Prosperity Fund
To support businesses to invest in resilience and growth, The Barclays Business Prosperity Fund is available for new and existing Business Banking customers and UK Corporate Banking clients across the UK to apply for lending and refinancing on existing projects.
£22bn is the total amount of lending Barclays has available to lend and support business growth among Business Banking and UK Corporate Banking clients in 2026. Subject to normal lending assessment, status and application. Terms and conditions apply.
Jason Constable, Head of Real Estate at Barclays UK Corporate Bank, said: “As extreme heat becomes a more regular operational challenge, UK firms are investing in practical measures to stay resilient, from cooling systems and workplace upgrades to energy efficiency to manage higher energy use and employee wellbeing. For consumer-facing businesses, cooler and more comfortable premises can also help protect footfall, dwell time and day-to-day trading during hotter periods.”
Constable added: “That presents a clear opportunity for heating and cooling, retrofitting, facilities management, and wider sustainability providers. As demand grows across both business and consumer markets, these sectors can play an important role in helping firms adapt, protect productivity and build long-term resilience.”
Gavin Parker, Head of Property Services at Barclays UK Corporate Bank, said: "As businesses invest in cooling, ventilation, energy efficiency and wider workplace upgrades, facilities management providers are well placed to help organisations adapt to the challenges of extreme heat.”
Parker continued: "From retrofit projects to improving building performance, the sector has a key role to play in helping businesses protect productivity and employee wellbeing. As demand for these services grows, access to finance to support expansion and investment will be critical. Through initiatives such as the Barclays Business Prosperity Fund, we're helping businesses invest in projects that strengthen resilience and support long-term growth."

full_text:
The heatwave boost fuelling summer sales cooled last month, as Brits cut back on retail spending to deal with rising bills.
Retail sales grew by 0.7 per cent in the year to August, marking a significant slowdown compared to 3.1 per cent growth in August 2025, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
August’s rate lagged below the 12-month average of 1.6 per cent growth, dragged down by lower spending on big-ticket items like furniture and household appliances.
High temperatures had put a rocket behind retail spending earlier this summer. While the record heat dampened high street footfall, Brits splurged on items like fans and barbecues through online sellers.
But this heatwave boost to consumer spending is cooling as autumn nears, the BRC has found.
Linda Ellett, head of consumer at KPMG – which produced the BRC’s data – said: “Despite temperatures remaining high, summer season cooled off for retail sales in August.”
Record heat caused Brits to kick off their summer spending early, meaning that sales of most categories excluding food and drink are set to run out of steam earlier than expected, she said.
Food sales jumped by 2.6 per cent in August. While lower than the 3.2 per cent 12-month average, this growth dragged up the headline sales figure.
Non-food sales fell by 0.8 per cent year on year in August, compared to the 12-month average of 0.2 per cent.
All eyes on Budget
Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the BRC, described August as a “disappointing” end to the summer for the UK’s retailers.
“With the cost of household bills rising, and set to rise further, many shoppers have clearly been tightening their belts.
“This was particularly true for discretionary spending, as big-ticket purchases like furniture and household appliances declined and consumers opted to instead treat themselves to smaller luxuries in health and beauty.”
Retailers are ramping up their demands on the government to slash their tax burden ahead of next month’s Budget.
Industry figures have called on Chancellor John Healey to unwind hikes to employer national insurance contributions and reform the business rates system, which they say is blighting the high street with closed-up shops.
“The new government has put high streets at the centre of their vision for better economic growth and the upcoming Budget is an opportunity to deliver on this commitment,” Dhillon said.
“Taking action on business rates and energy costs would help support retail investment in local communities while delivering value for consumers.”

full_text:
The National Weather Service is warning that a midweek heat wave will likely bring triple-digit temperatures to inland Humboldt County — temperatures accompanied by elevated heat risk.
“A strong ridge of high pressure will develop over the Desert Southwest next week, bringing a rapid increase in temperatures beginning Monday,” NWS’s Eureka office announced this Sunday via social media. “The warmest conditions are expected Wednesday through Thursday, when Moderate HeatRisk will exist in portions of the area. This includes locations closer to the coast that have not experienced temperatures this warm so far this season.”
Locations like Willow Creek, Hoopa and Garberville could see temperatures in excess of 100 degrees. Along the coast, temperatures in communities like Eureka may creep into the 70s, with weather in the Eel River Valley entering the high-70s and communities like Petrolia even breaking 80 degrees.
Heat risk will be concentrated in inland areas, where heat-sensitive groups and persons not acclimated to high heat should exercise caution.
NWS recommends reducing time in the sun during the warmest part of the day, staying hydrated and in a cool place during the heat of the day, scheduling outdoor activities for cooler parts of the day and, for those that might be at elevated risk because of a lack of air conditioning, using fans to keep air moving and open windows at night.
Concerned residents can call 211 and reach out to the county’s Emergency Weather Community Response Network for information on cooling centers and resources to avoid extreme heat. Holiday hours may affect the county’s ability to respond.
